A self-taught painter and printmaker of the School of Tunis, Dhahak occupies a singular position: formed between Tunisian tradition and European modernism. 
His Roman training (1957–61) under Amerigo Bartoli and Macari proved decisive, culminating in the Carlo Giviera Prize. Returning to Tunisia, he asserted artistic independence after teaching in Sfax. From his first Tunis solo show (1964) to the Cité des Arts, Paris (1972), and his Sidi Bou Saïd printmaking studio, his practice unites technical rigor with a profoundly Mediterranean sensitivity—recognized by the Grand Prix de Tunis (1991) and the National Prize for Plastic Arts (1994).

ocr:
Brahim Dhahak
Self-taught painter and printmaker — between
Tunis, Rome, and Paris
A self-taught painter and member of the School of
Tunis, he attended Rome's Artistic Academy from
1957 to 1961, a decisive period that transformed
him into an accomplished master. Studying under
Amerigo Bartoli and master printmaker Macari, he
refined his technique and won the Carlo Giviera
Prize in 1961.
Returning to Tunisia at 30, he taught drawing
in Sfax. Shorty after, he left to preserve his
independence. His first solo exhibition was held in
Tunis in 1964, before a stay at the Cité des Arts in
Paris in 1972. From then on, he exhibited regularly
in Tunisia and abroad, in the context of solo and
group exhibitions.
An accomplished printmaker, he produced an
important body of work in this field in his studio in
Sidi Bou Said. His creations earned him the Grand
Prix of the City of Tunis in 1991, and then the
National Prize for Plastic Arts in 1994.
Brahim Dhahak embodies the image of a complete
artist, nourished by the dialogue between
Tunisian tradition and European know-how,
whose technical rigor is allied with a profoundly
Mediterranean sensitivity.
